power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p>.05", Text = "Most of the classifiers cannot discriminate the gender and neither a feature set nor a classification algorithm or a training setup has a distinct advantage over the other (all p>.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p>.05", Sentence = "Most of the classifiers cannot discriminate the gender and neither a feature set nor a classification algorithm or a training setup has a distinct advantage over the other (all p>.05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond.

Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies.

This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data.
Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations.
Gender classification served as a proofof-concept downstream analysis.
Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information.
Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0.
Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations.
Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established.

These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features.

The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations.
Quantification of the human gait is of interest to a variety of disciplines.

In the wider context of health, gait features can on the medical side support the diagnostic procedure and monitoring of disorder or therapeutic progress [1] in orthopaedics [1] [2] [3], neurology (e.g., Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease [4, 5] or stroke [6]), and psychiatry (e.g., schizophrenia, anxiety, depression, and other mood disorder [7] [8] [9] [10]).

This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and processing pipeline for harmonizing heterogeneous accelerometer data acquired during walking.

The technical framework integrates participant-, study-, sensor-, and recording-specific information with standardized processing steps for gait-cycle extraction, quality assessment, and feature generation.

Across six publicly available datasets, the results demonstrate that such a framework can substantially reduce technical heterogeneity and enable joint analysis of data originating from different studies.
At the same time, the analyses show that technical harmonization does not necessarily result in comparable resulting gait representations.
Residual differences related to dataset, sensor location, and body side remain evident, both for normalized gait cycles and for derived statistical features.
This distinction between harmonization of data processing and comparability of the underlying measurements presents important implications for cross-study gait analysis.
The results from the statistical evaluation demonstrate that data can be represented in a common analytical format but still lack analytical comparability.

For example, accelerometer recordings obtained from the right waist in the OU-ISIR-SAID [55] and Vajdi [53] datasets were processed using the same pipeline and nominally represent the same sensor location, yet the resulting average gait cycles show only moderate correspondence, while several statistical features differ substantially.

text.text: This finding indicates that differences between studies cannot be attributed solely to data format or preprocessing.
Rather, sensor characteristics, recording protocols, participant populations, and other study-specific factors may remain embedded in the resulting features even after standardized processing.

Therefore, technical harmonization is a necessary first step for creating a common representation in which residual heterogeneity can be quantified and investigated, rather than a procedure that completely removes heterogeneity.
This issue is well known in other modalities, e.g., batch effects in genomics data [62, 63] or scanner effects in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [64] [65] [66] [67] [68].

text.text: While those approaches may be suitable for the statistical features derived from the accelerometer data, the partially distinct forms of the unified gait cycles suggest that this feature might not be fit for combination across datasets.
These considerations are particularly relevant for multi-study analyses, where apparently standardized inputs may still contain systematic study-or devicespecific information.
The results furthermore suggest that harmonization strategies have to explicitly retain sensor location information as an important characteristic of the signal.

Data recorded at different body locations are influenced by different biomechanical components of body motion [69, 70] and are therefore not expected to exhibit identical temporal or statistical characteristics even after normalization.

text.text: Our correlation analysis indicates generally stronger correspondence among centrally positioned sensors, even across datasets, whereas sensors located toward the extremities, such as the ankle and wrist, tend to show lower correspondence with sensors positioned closer to the body center or with sensors from other datasets.
This renders the former especially suitable for analyses across datasets.
However, depending on the use case, the former or latter is better suited to capture the characteristic of interest [72].

text.text: The pairwise comparisons demonstrate that some sensor-position combinations have substantially stronger correspondence, indicating that harmonization can facilitate meaningful comparisons under appropriate conditions.
The across-and within-subject analyses provide additional evidence that the magnitude of variability depends on both the dataset and the sensor configuration.
In several datasets, across-subject correlations were higher than the corresponding within-subject variability, whereas other datasets showed the opposite pattern.
This heterogeneity suggests that the relative contributions of subject-specific gait characteristics and recording-specific factors are not constant across datasets.
Consequently, pooled analyses should account for the individual structure of the data and only opt for a combination of datasets when the conditions are met.
The gait-cycle extraction procedure provides an important foundation for our harmonization approach.
When evaluated against annotated gait events in the MAREA dataset [52], dominant-peak detection showed high accuracy for both left and right ankle sensors, with mean accuracies over 99%.

text.text: These findings support the feasibility of extracting a consistent gait-cycle representation directly from single sensor accelerometer recordings, even when explicit gait-cycle annotations are unavailable.
However, this validation should be interpreted within the scope of the available ground truth.

The algorithm was evaluated against event annotations from a single dataset and only for ankle-mounted sensors; therefore, these results do not establish equivalent performance across all sensor positions represented in the data warehouse.
This limitation is particularly relevant for peripheral and non-peripheral sensors, for which the relationship between local acceleration patterns and conventional gait events may differ.
Future validation using independently annotated datasets and multiple sensor locations would therefore be important to establish the generalizability of the extraction algorithm.

Along this line, we decided for a unified processing of the data from each sensor individually instead of a global gait cycle extraction across sensors because of the heterogeneity in number of sensors and their locations across datasets.

An extension of the preprocessing pipeline might be useful for specific sets of sensors when a global gait cycle with temporally aligned sensor cycles is necessary for addressing specific research questions.
The quality-control procedure offers a complementary safeguard against unreliable cycle extraction.
Of the 343,431 extracted gait cycles, 74.4% met the predefined correlation threshold of 0.7 with the corresponding mean gait cycle and were retained for downstream analysis.
This demonstrates the practical value of an automated quality-assessment step when integrating data from heterogeneous sources.

At the same time, the finding that approximately one quarter of all extracted cycles did not meet the criterion indicates that the choice of quality threshold has a potentially substantial effect on the resulting analytical dataset.
The threshold of 0.7 was selected for the present analysis and is configurable in the pipeline.
Nevertheless, the current study does not establish whether this threshold is optimal across datasets, sensor locations, or gait conditions.
The within-subject correlations demonstrate substantial differences for sensor positions and datasets suggesting that it might be recommended to adapt individual thresholds.
Importantly, however, a low correlation with the mean cycle is not necessarily equivalent to poor data quality, as atypical but genuine gait cycles may also differ from the recording-specific mean.
Especially in clinical populations, this variability can even be an important feature of interest [74] [75] [76].

text.text: The rational for the gender-classification analysis was to provide a proof of concept for the use of the harmonized data in downstream analysis, rather than to develop an optimized gender-classification model.
Classification performance was generally close to chance for the examined sensors, and a consistent benefit from combining data across datasets or sensor locations could therefore not be established.
These findings do not demonstrate that the harmonization framework is ineffective.
Rather, they illustrate that successful technical harmonization does not automatically translate into improved performance in a downstream machine-learning task.
Furthermore, the configuration of the six training setups provides a suitable strategy for proper evaluation of joint data usage.

Comparing the power of the increased data size achieved by pooling with the performance of the individual datasets and the pooled data while keeping dataset size provides a comprehensive test for improvement via data pooling.
Training on one dataset and testing on the other provides a test unbiased to preprocessing for the generalizability across studies.

The strength of this study is the use of multiple publicly available datasets with substantial variation in participant numbers, recording duration, sensor type, sensor location, and study characteristics.
This heterogeneity reflects the conditions under which a general harmonization framework ultimately needs to operate.

The data warehouse additionally retains contextual information alongside the sensor measurements, providing a basis for investigating these sources of variation rather than discarding them during preprocessing.

The framework is also designed to accommodate additional processing steps, sensor modalities and further datasets, while the technical artifacts are provided in an open-source toolbox with accompanying documentation.
These endeavours support reproducibility and provide a basis for extending the framework beyond the datasets evaluated here.
Some limitations, nevertheless, need to be considered.

First, the available datasets differed substantially in participant characteristics, recording duration, sensor configuration, and study protocol, and these factors are often intrinsically confounded.

For example, an observed dataset effect cannot necessarily be attributed to the dataset itself because it may reflect differences in hardware, placement, participant population, or recording conditions.
Second, several potentially informative comparisons could not be performed because the required metadata or features were unavailable.
Consequently, the pairwise comparisons should be regarded as representative examples rather than a complete characterization of all possible sources of heterogeneity.
Future studies might explicitly model contextual factors such as age, footwear, walking surface, and other recording conditions in order to disentangle their contributions [77].
text.formatted: Future studies might explicitly model contextual factors such as age, footwear, walking surface, and other recording conditions in order to disentangle their contributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">[77]</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the present study demonstrates that heterogeneous accelerometer datasets can be integrated into a common analytical framework with standardized gait-cycle extraction, quality management, and feature engineering.
At the same time, the results show that technical harmonization alone does not remove systematic differences associated with datasets and sensor configurations.

The principal contribution of the framework is therefore to provide a reproducible infrastructure in which the differences across datasets can be identified, quantified, and incorporated into subsequent analyses.

Such an approach facilitates more transparent cross-study comparisons, reproducible feature engineering, and ultimately more robust development and validation of gait-analysis methods across heterogeneous real-world datasets.

text.text: In this structure, one or more central fact tables store the primary observational data while multiple dimension tables provide contextual information relevant to those observations.
Each dimension table is directly associated with one or more fact tables, and the dimensions are independent from each other.
In contrast to normalized relational designs, the star schema intentionally permits a certain degree of data redundancy to simplify query operations.

By reducing the number of required joins, this approach improves computational efficiency at data read-out and is therefore well suited for analytical environments that demand rapid processing of large and complex datasets.
The implemented scheme includes four initial fact tables: Raw Accelerometer, Raw Gyroscope, Raw Magnetometer, and Raw EMG.
Only the raw accelerometer data is further processed.
They store the respective raw sensor readings together with timestamps to maintain temporal order.

Additional fact tables, introduced during feature extraction, are the preprocessed accelerometer data, extracted gait cycles in different normalization steps as well as statistical features extracted from the gait cycles.

Eight dimension tables provide complementary information on activities (activity), ground conditions (ground), participants (person), recording metadata (recording), technical sensor information (sensor), sensor placement (sensor_location), step events (step_event), and rotation information for harmonization of sensors (world_coordinate_system).
A comprehensive description of the data model, including a detailed data dictionary, is available in the accompanying technical documentation.
SQL scripts for setting up the data scheme with a postgreSQL (The PostgreSQL Global Development Group) database are provided in the code repository.

The initial ETL process incorporates the full set of available sensor data, resulting in a raw dataset that includes accelerometer measurements from walking and non-walking activities as well as data from additional sensor modalities.
Depending on the specific research objectives, the processing pipeline may be extended to accommodate further activity types, facilitated by the accompanying data dictionary.

The data itself is not included as part of the code package and needs to be obtained independently since some of the datasets are only available upon request from the researchers who recorded the data.
Moreover, the data warehouse is designed to easily integrate additional recordings, enabling researchers to enrich the repository with their own data if required.
The analysis focusses on gait cycles derived from the accelerometer data during walking.
Because most available datasets do not explicitly provide gait cycle annotations, we designed and tested an algorithm to extract gait cycles directly from the sensor signals.

Each accelerometer provides tri-axial measurements (𝑥, 𝑦, and 𝑧 components), which inherently depend on the sensor's orientation, as each axis captures acceleration along a specific spatial direction.
To mitigate this orientation dependency and obtain a signal representation that reflects only the underlying dynamic behaviour, the Euclidean norm of the jerk is used for further processing.
To estimate the global step frequency, we identified the first prominent peak in the frequency spectrum.
For sensor placements near the body's center of mass, this peak typically appears around 2 Hz, whereas peripheral sensor locations yield frequencies closer to 1 Hz.

For non-centered sensor placements, a gait cycle is defined as the concatenation of the swing phase of the limb bearing the sensor, resulting in a dominant peak, followed by the contralateral swing phase, which yields a non-dominant peak.
Dominant peaks are first identified by locating local maxima that exceed the global mean, while enforcing a minimum inter-peak distance determined by the estimated step frequency.
To suppress non-dominant events among these candidates, we apply an amplitude threshold derived from the mean of the candidate peak amplitudes, again subject to the same distance constraint.

Assuming an alternating dominant/non-dominant structure, we subsequently examine the inter-peak intervals with respect to the step period to infer and insert missing dominant peaks whose amplitudes may fall below the mean-based threshold.
Non-dominant peaks are then identified by segmenting the signal between successive dominant peaks under the assumption that each segment contains exactly one non-dominant event.
Because this event lies between two flanking minima, it is designated as the maximum bounded by the pair of 'major minima' (Fig 9).
text.formatted: Because this event lies between two flanking minima, it is designated as the maximum bounded by the pair of 'major minima' (Fig <ref type="figure">9</ref>).

text.text: To determine these minima, we first detect all local minima within the segment, excluding those within a small neighbourhood of dominant peaks to avoid false detections.
The absolute minimum in the segment is taken as the first major minimum.
For each remaining candidate minimum, we compute the highest signal value along the path connecting it to the absolute minimum.
Minima that lie in the same valley as the absolute minimum yield lower connecting maxima, whereas those positioned across the opposing valley share the amplitude of the non-dominant peak.
Among the minima belonging to this opposing valley, the one with the lowest value is selected as the second major minimum.
The non-dominant peak is then identified as the highest local maximum located between these two major minima.
The gait cycle is then defined as the major minimum preceding the dominant peak until the major minimum preceding the next dominant peak.
All detected minima are marked with a circle.
The first minimum is simply the lowest value (hot pink).
The second minimum is not the second lowest value since this can be on the same side of the non-dominant peak.
The algorithm described in the text finds the true second minimum (dark purple).
For centrally mounted sensors, the extraction of individual gait cycles is accomplished by segmenting the signal at every second minimum between successive peaks.
This approach is feasible because contributions from the left and right leg appear with comparable prominence in the signal, resulting in a symmetric pattern that allows reliable cycle delineation.
To evaluate the performance of the cycle extraction algorithm, we used the ankle-mounted sensors from the MAREA dataset, which provide annotated step-event labels.
Heel-strike events are expected to correspond, with a temporal offset, to the dominant and non-dominant peaks identified within the extracted gait cycles.
However, because the dataset occasionally contains misordered event annotations, only walking sequences with correctly ordered step-event labels are included in the analysis.

Wrist-mounted accelerometer data are excluded, as the dominant peak observed in wrist motion during a gait cycle is not temporally aligned with the heel strike and therefore does not constitute a reliable reference event.
Because heel-strike annotations and signal-derived peak positions do not coincide perfectly, a tolerance threshold was defined to account for minor temporal deviations.

Based on typical step frequencies and the dataset's sampling rate, a maximum difference of 123 milliseconds between the detected peak and the annotated ground-truth event was established as an acceptable margin of error.
To identify gait cycles unsuitable for inclusion in further analysis including the calculation of statistical features, a quality-assessment procedure was implemented.
A mean gait cycle was computed for each recording, each participant, and each dataset, separately for each sensor location.
In datasets where only a single recording was available per participant, the mean gait cycle at the recording and participant levels was identical.
Cycles exceeding a predefined correlation threshold with their respective mean gait cycle were retained for further analysis, whereas those falling below the threshold were excluded.
In this study, a correlation coefficient of 0.7 was selected as the cutoff threshold for inclusion.

To evaluate the comparability of the uniform gait cycles, we computed Pearson correlation coefficients between all combinations of sensor locations and datasets.
For each of those combinations we firstly calculate the average cycle per participant and then average those cycles for the further calculations.
This analysis was performed separately for centered and non-centered sensor positions.
Furthermore, to characterize variability at the participant level, we conducted an analysis for each dataset-sensor-location combination.

Specifically, we calculated the average correlation among the uniform gait cycles of different participants (across subject correlation) and compared these values with the correlations obtained among cycles belonging to the same participant (within subject correlation).
This comparison provides insight into the extent to which gait-cycle representations are consistent within individuals relative to variability across individuals.

text.text: For the classification analyses, we used two machine learning algorithms: logistic regression as a linear classifier and random forests as a nonlinear classifier.
The same two feature sets as in the statistical analysis were evaluated: (i) the ten statistical features and (ii) ten features derived from the uniform gait cycles (see below).
Six training-testing strategies were examined.

These included training and testing on data from a single sensor; training and testing on combined data from both sensors, either preserving the dataset size of a single sensor or doubling it; and training on one sensor while testing on the other.
For all six strategies, the amount of training data was matched to the size of the smaller dataset to ensure comparability across conditions.
The data was sampled once in the beginning of the analysis, so all six strategies relied on the same participants.

To harmonize the dimensionality across feature sets, we used the first ten principal components derived from a principal component analysis (PCA) calculated on ten randomly chosen gait cycles per participant and condition.
Classification performance was evaluated using stratified cross-validation.
To ensure statistical reliability, each fold contained a minimum of five samples, with the total number of folds capped at ten.
For comparisons that yielded less than five folds we only report the balanced accuracy over all folds, for the remaining comparison we calculated mean and standard deviation across folds.

Stratification was performed primarily with respect to gender, and in cases when data from two sources were combined also with respect to the originating dataset, to the extent permitted by the available sample distributions.
To assess whether classification performance exceeded chance level, we conducted one-sided t-tests against chance level of 0.5.
This test was skipped if the data was partitioned in less than five folds.
A conservative significance threshold of α = 0.01 was chosen to account for the multiple comparisons inherent in the evaluation across classifiers, feature sets, and training strategies.
For completeness, results achieving only a threshold of α = 0.05 or even exceeding α = 0.001 are also indicated.
In cases where the number of available folds was insufficient to support a t-test, we instead reported the weighted mean of the fold-wise accuracies as a descriptive summary measure.

To evaluate the influence of classification algorithm, feature set, and training strategy on model performance, we conducted mixed-effects analyses of variance (ANOVA) on the accuracy outcomes, with classification algorithm as within-subject factor and feature set as well as training-testing strategy as between-subject factors.
